rows: Employers must assess tasks involving products that contain isocyanates.
Spraying can create very high inhalation exposure to isocyanates.
Risk assessment should identify who may be exposed, including nearby workers and members of the public.
Product labels and safety data sheets should be checked for isocyanates and other hazardous substances.
Lower-emission application methods should be used where practicable.
Spraying should be enclosed and extracted where possible.
Suitable air-fed breathing apparatus may be required for spraying.
Health surveillance and biological monitoring can be needed to confirm controls remain effective.
A product category or spray-booth record does not establish actual isocyanate exposure.
Exposure conclusions require formulation, task, aerosol generation, enclosure, clearance time, RPE and monitoring evidence.
Employers have a legal duty to assess risks from work-related stress.
Employers should act on significant stress risks identified by assessment.
Work-related stress can arise when workers cannot cope with excessive pressures or demands.
Work demands should be matched to workers' skills, knowledge and available time.
Workers and their representatives should be involved in identifying causes and improvements.
Organisational data and worker feedback can help identify stress patterns.
Controls should address underlying work design rather than rely only on individual coping.
Stress assessments should be reviewed when work organisation or workforce conditions change.
A sickness absence or performance change does not by itself prove that work caused stress.
Conclusions require worker consultation, demands, control, support, relationships, role, change and non-work context.
Employers should manage fatigue as a health and safety risk.
A fatigue risk-management system can help identify and control fatigue hazards.
Working-time limits do not replace a suitable fatigue risk assessment.
Long hours and poorly designed shifts can contribute to sleep debt.
Shift design should consider rotation, recovery time and consecutive duties.
Fatigue controls should address major-accident and routine operational risks.
Workers should be able to report fatigue concerns without undermining other controls.
Fatigue arrangements should be monitored and reviewed using operational evidence.
A rota or total weekly hours alone does not determine an individual's fatigue risk.
Risk conclusions require sleep opportunity, shift timing, workload, commute, recovery, health and task-criticality evidence.
Employers must consult employees about health and safety.
Consultation may be direct or through recognised or elected representatives as applicable.
Consultation should help develop and maintain effective safety measures.
Workers should receive enough information to participate meaningfully.
Employees should be able to raise concerns and influence decisions.
Consultation should cover proposed changes that may affect health and safety.
Representatives need suitable time, information and support for their functions.
Consultation arrangements should be reviewed to ensure they remain effective.
A committee meeting or policy document does not prove effective workforce consultation.
Effectiveness requires evidence of timely information, worker participation, responses, decisions and follow-through.
